drills.q: Given weights, values, and capacity W, write the recurrence for max value using each item at most once.
drills.a: dp[i][w] = max(dp[i-1][w], dp[i-1][w-wt[i]]+val[i]) when wt[i]<=w, else dp[i-1][w].

drills.q: Collapse the 2D 0/1 knapsack table to 1D. Which direction do you iterate capacity and why?
drills.a: Backward, from W down to wt[i]. Forward iteration would read a value already updated by this item in the same pass, letting it be counted twice.

drills.q: Determine whether an array can be partitioned into two subsets of equal sum.
drills.a: If total is odd, impossible. Otherwise run boolean subset-sum DP for target=total/2 with backward capacity iteration; dp[0]=True.

drills.q: Count the number of ways to assign +/- signs to an array to reach a target sum.
drills.a: Reduce to subset sum: P=(total+target)/2 must be a non-negative integer <= total; count subsets summing to P via dp[w] += dp[w-n].

drills.q: Extend 0/1 knapsack to two independent budgets (e.g. at most m zeros and n ones). What changes?
drills.a: Add a second capacity axis: dp[i][j] = max(dp[i][j], dp[i-cost0][j-cost1]+1); both axes must be iterated backward per item, same once-only argument per axis.

drills.q: An item has a bounded count c (not 1, not infinite). How do you solve bounded knapsack without an O(n*W*c) blowup?
drills.a: Decompose each item into O(log c) meta-items via binary/power-of-two split (sizes 1,2,4,...,remainder), then run standard 0/1 knapsack on the expanded item list in O(n*W*log c).
